title: Linear-time directed shortest paths with nonnegative real weights
formal: Do there exist an integer word-size constant \(B\ge3\), an absolute constant \(K>0\), and one uniform deterministic comparison-addition RAM algorithm that, on every explicitly given simple directed graph with \(n\ge2\) vertices and \(m\) arcs of arbitrary nonnegative real lengths, and every specified source vertex, outputs all exact source distances within \(K(n+m)\) instructions? The model below charges control, memory access, preprocessing and output as well as operations on real values.
definitions:
The graph has vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), no loops and at most one arc for each ordered pair of distinct vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. Input consists of \(n,m\), a source \(s\in[n]\), and an arbitrary-order explicit list of all arcs, each with its two integer endpoints and one exact real length \(w_e\ge0\). There is no bound on real magnitudes or rationality. Zero lengths, zero-length cycles, disconnected graphs and vertices unreachable from the source are allowed.

A directed walk from \(s\) to \(v\) follows arcs in their given directions and has length equal to the sum of their lengths. The empty walk has length zero. For a reachable vertex, its distance is the minimum of these lengths; nonnegative weights allow repeated vertices to be removed without increasing length, so a minimum is attained by a simple path, or by the empty path when \(v=s\). An unreachable vertex has distance \(+\infty\). The output is an array indexed by \([n]\), containing each exact finite distance or a distinct infinity marker. No sorted order of distances is requested, and an unevaluated implicit distance expression is not the output.

The machine has integer control words of \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits and separately typed exact-real cells. Integer addresses must fit a word. An instruction can read or write one cell, copy a value, compare values of the same type and branch. Integer instructions also include Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and quotient or remainder by a nonzero word. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Multiword computations pay for their constituent instructions.

Real instructions are copying, comparison, addition and subtraction, each of unit cost. Finitely many rational program constants are allowed. There is no real multiplication or division, rounding, floor, access to digits or bits, or conversion of an input-dependent real value to an integer. Real values cannot serve as addresses. Integer instructions cannot inspect real encodings. The saved subtraction convention can be represented with pairs of sums and comparisons of such pairs; it does not supply multiplication or encoding access. The infinity output is a separate tag and is not treated as a real operand.

One finite program and the constants \(B,K\) work for all \(n,m,s\), graphs and real inputs. There are no random bits, advice strings, precomputed input-dependent tables or free oracles. Every executed instruction counts, including graph preprocessing, initialization of working storage, control and address arithmetic, and writing the \(n\) outputs. Table construction is charged. Time is worst-case over all inputs, and includes every operation needed to choose the next real comparison or sum; bounding only the number of real arithmetic operations is insufficient. The algorithm must halt correctly on every allowed input. The linear bound is uniform over real edge values and graph density.

context_blocks.text: The output associates a distance with each named vertex. It need not sort vertices by those distances, so a sorting lower bound does not automatically apply.
The real-weight model forbids integer bit tricks on edge lengths. A linear-time algorithm must instead organize comparisons and sums while also paying for graph access and control.

Counting only numerical operations can hide expensive decisions about which operation to perform next. The explicit total-instruction criterion preserves the algorithmic milestone selected for this card.

why: An optimal linear algorithm would determine whether directed shortest paths with general nonnegative numerical lengths can be computed at the cost of reading the graph.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of a program and constants with the stated all-input bound, or prove its logical negation in exactly this model. A one-sided improvement above linear time, a result only for undirected graphs or integer weights, or a bound that excludes control and preprocessing time does not suffice. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion unless the condition is also proved.

progress.text: The deterministic \(O(m(\log n)^{2/3})\) theorem breaks the previous sorting barrier on sparse directed instances. An additive \(O(n)\) scan accounts for arbitrary explicit isolated vertices.
Theorem 1 improves the nontrivial directed bound to \(O(m\sqrt{\log n}+\sqrt{mn\log n\log\log n})\) in the source’s graph regime; it still does not yield total \(O(m+n)\) time on every graph.

A new preprint studies exact optima for charged numerical operations. Its introduction explicitly permits exponentially costly policy selection, so that guarantee is not total linear RAM time. The reported theorems were checked for scope, not independently audited.
A separate new speedup concerns undirected graphs and retains logarithmic factors. It does not establish the selected directed linear-time target.

status_note: The checked July 2026 directed result still has superlinear factors. September developments concern either undirected inputs or a numerical-operation cost that can omit expensive policy selection. Neither establishes this user-selected total linear-time target. This source and bounded later-work review through 18 September 2026 is not an exhaustive certification or independent proof audit.

sentences: The task is to compute every exact distance from one source in a directed graph with nonnegative real arc lengths.
The requested running time is linear in the number of vertices and arcs.
A uniform deterministic machine may compare, add and subtract real values but cannot inspect their encodings.
All memory access, control, preprocessing and output instructions count toward the bound.
Recent improvements and separate numerical-operation results leave this total-time milestone unanswered in the checked sources.
